svg.text: What is Machine Learning? Supervised vs Unsupervised 🤖
ML = giving a computer the ability to learn patterns from data, without being programmed for every case. Two main families:
supervised (learn from labeled "right answers") and unsupervised (find hidden structure in unlabeled data).
📖 What is ML? (Arthur Samuel, 1959)
Definition: "the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed."
🎲 The checkers story: Samuel was not a great player. He let a program play tens of thousands of games against itself,
learn which board positions lead to wins vs losses, and it became better than Samuel himself. Lesson: more data → better.
The big families of ML: supervised · unsupervised · recommender systems · reinforcement learning. This note covers the first two.
🎯 Supervised learning: learn from labeled "right answers" (X → Y)
You give the algorithm examples that include the correct answer — the label Y for each input X. After training on many
(X, Y) pairs, it can predict Y for a brand-new X it has never seen.
Everyday examples (input X → output Y):
📧 Spam filter: email → spam? 🎙️ Speech: audio → text 🌐 Translate: English → Spanish
📢 Online ads: ad + you → click? 🚗 Self-driving: image → car positions 🔍 Inspection: photo → defect?
📈 Regression → predict a NUMBER
Out of infinitely many numbers. Example: house
price from size (fit a line or a curve). Could be
$150k, $183k, or anything in between.
🏷️ Classification → predict a CATEGORY
From a small, fixed set. Example: tumor benign (0)
vs malignant (1); cat vs dog. Can be more than 2
classes, and can use many inputs (age + size…).
Key difference: regression predicts any number (infinite choices) · classification predicts one of a few fixed categories.
🔍 Unsupervised learning: find structure in UNLABELED data (X only, no Y)
The data comes with only inputs X, no labels Y. The algorithm must find structure / patterns on its own. Three types:
🧩 Clustering
Group similar points together.
Google News groups articles by shared
words (panda / twin / zoo) with no human
labels. Also: customer market segments.
🚨 Anomaly detection
Find unusual data points.
A strange point stands out from the rest.
Used for fraud detection — a weird
transaction is a possible sign of fraud.
🗜️ Dimensionality reduction
Compress a big dataset into fewer
numbers, losing as little info as possible.
Smaller data = cheaper to store and
faster to search.
⚖️ The one contrast to remember (the tumor example)
Supervised → data is LABELED (X, Y)
age
Each point is labeled (◯ benign,
✕ malignant). It learns a boundary.
→ Regression & Classification
Goal: reproduce known answers
for new inputs.
Unsupervised → NO labels (X only)
age
No labels given. The model finds
groups / structure itself.
→ Clustering · Anomaly · Dim-reduction
Goal: discover patterns nobody
told it about in advance.
📡 Why this matters for you (the link to the LLM course you already did)
🔗 An LLM (GPT / Claude) is trained with "self-supervised learning" — a clever form of supervised learning
Next-token prediction turns plain text into a supervised problem: input X = the words so far, label Y = the next word — and
that label comes straight from the text itself, so no human has to label anything. That is why it scales to the whole internet.
So a chatbot is, at heart, a giant classification over tokens (pick the next token). 2026 twist: multi-token prediction (draft
several tokens per step for speed). And clustering + dimensionality reduction are exactly what power RAG search and quantization.
🔑 The bedrock to keep:
Everything in modern AI — LLMs, RAG, reasoning — still reduces to one idea: learn a function from data. The 4 big families:
supervised (labeled) · unsupervised (find structure) · recommender systems · reinforcement learning (learn from rewards — how
reasoning models are trained). You now have the map; the rest of this course fills it in.
